::: {.why}
Storing adjusted prices bakes today's history into the file and makes yesterday's file disagree with today's; computing the adjustment on read costs microseconds and never lies.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Explain why a stored adjusted-close column is wrong the moment the next dividend is paid.
- Return a total-return series and a raw price series from the same store with one function and a flag.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Write qlib/store.py's `bars(security, start, end, adjust=True)`: join bar_daily to corporate_action, compute the cumulative adjustment factor from the end of the window backwards, and apply it. Reuse the arithmetic you validated on day 16.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Test it against the reference: your adjusted SPY series against yfinance's `auto_adjust=True`, over 2005-today, and assert the maximum relative difference is under a tolerance you choose and state. When they disagree, the dividend timing convention is the usual culprit.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The store can now return both a raw price series and a total-return series from the same rows, with adjustment computed at read time. That choice is what will let a backtest run in March against the same file you ingested in September without the history having quietly moved.
:::
